questions.q: In the illustrative data, what share of won revenue comes from deals over $75K?
questions.explain: $2.67M of $6.30M is about 42%, even though those deals are only 21% of won deals (30 of 140).

questions.q: Which report feature groups deals into ranges like under $25K, $25K to $75K, and over $75K without changing any data?
questions.explain: Bucket columns group numeric values into ranges inside a report.

questions.q: Why is sales cycle length a report or formula job rather than a SOQL job, per this lesson?
options: SOQL cannot subtract one date field from another inside a query
Dates are not stored on opportunities
questions.explain: SOQL filters and aggregates, but arithmetic between fields such as Close Date minus Created Date is done in a report formula or a formula field.

questions.q: Which is a real data limitation the lesson warns about when measuring cycle length?
options: Salesforce always rounds cycles to 30 days
Close Date is entered by people and can be backdated or slid, skewing cycle length
questions.explain: Close Date is user-entered, so cycles built from it should be spot-checked against created dates and stage history.

questions.q: Large deals average about 96 days to close. A large deal was created two weeks ago and is marked to close this quarter with three weeks left. What is the sensible conclusion?
options: It will certainly close because the close date says so
It carries serious timing risk and should not be counted on for this quarter
It proves the average cycle is wrong
questions.explain: Against a typical 96-day cycle, a deal that young is unlikely to close within three weeks, whatever its close date says.
